items.prompt: What does the abbreviation SEO stand for in digital marketing?

options.label: Social engagement outreach
Site evaluation overview
Sales email operations
Search engine optimization

rubric: SEO means search engine optimization: improving a site's visibility in unpaid search results.
Other options are invented expansions that sound plausible.

items.prompt: What does CTR measure in an online ad campaign?

options.label: Share of ad viewers who clicked it
Average cost the advertiser pays per sale made
Number of times the ad was shown to people
Total money spent on the ad over the campaign

rubric: Click-through rate is clicks divided by impressions.
Distractors confuse CTR with cost, spend or impressions.

items.prompt: Which term describes the text a user clicks to subscribe to or buy from a page, such as 'Buy now' or 'Sign up'?

options.label: Impression
Meta description
Call to action
Backlink

rubric: A call to action prompts the next step.
Meta descriptions and backlinks are SEO elements; impressions are a count of displays.

items.prompt: In paid search, what does PPC stand for?

options.label: Posts per campaign
Pay per click
Profit per customer
Page position control

rubric: PPC means pay per click: the advertiser pays when someone clicks the ad.
Other options are plausible-sounding but wrong expansions.

items.prompt: Which of these is an email marketing metric that shows the share of sent emails that were opened?

options.label: Open rate
Bounce rate
Unsubscribe rate
Conversion rate

rubric: Open rate is opens divided by delivered emails.
Bounce rate counts undelivered emails; conversion and unsubscribe measure other actions.

items.prompt: Which of the following are online channels commonly used in digital marketing? Select all that apply.

options.label: Search engine ads
Printed street billboards
Email newsletters
Printed newspaper inserts

items.prompt: A small bakery owner launches a website and wants to track how many visitors complete a purchase. A friend says there is a specific term for the share of visitors who take a desired action such as buying. What is that term?

options.label: Reach
Impression share
Bounce rate
Conversion rate

rubric: Conversion rate is the share of visitors completing a goal action.
Bounce rate is single-page exits; reach and impression share count exposure.

items.prompt: Why do marketers set a specific goal, such as 200 newsletter sign-ups in a month, before starting a campaign?

options.label: It lowers the price per click that ad platforms charge
It means results need checking only once the campaign ends
It lets them judge afterwards whether the campaign worked
It guarantees the campaign will reach that sign-up number

rubric: A clear goal gives a benchmark for judging results.
Goals do not guarantee outcomes, replace tracking or change ad prices.

items.prompt: What is the main difference between organic and paid reach on social media?

options.label: Organic reach is always larger than paid reach, because paid ads are shown to fewer people
Organic reach comes from email subscribers, while paid reach comes from search engine results
Organic reach applies only to video posts, while paid reach applies only to text-based posts
Organic reach comes without paying for ads; paid reach comes from ad spend

rubric: Organic reach is unpaid exposure; paid reach is bought through ads.
Other options invent format or channel splits or claim fixed size.

items.prompt: A user types 'running shoes' into a search engine. Which result is best described as an organic result?

options.label: A listing labeled 'Ad' at the top of the results page
A page ranked because its content matches the search
A banner for the same shoes shown on another site later
A sponsored product carousel with prices and photos

rubric: Organic results are ranked by relevance, not payment.
Labeled ads, sponsored items and retargeting banners are paid.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to segment an email list, for example by customer interests?

options.label: Segments guarantee that no one unsubscribes
Segments remove the need to write a subject line
Segments let emails bypass spam filters automatically
Each group gets messages that fit it better

rubric: Segmentation improves relevance of messages.
It does not bypass spam filters, replace subject lines or prevent unsubscribes.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why a campaign uses several channels, such as search, social and email together?

options.label: Each channel costs the same per customer, so splitting the budget evenly lowers the total spend
Different channels reach people at different moments and reinforce each other
Ad platforms usually limit each advertiser to one channel, so a campaign must spread across several
Running more channels at once raises sales, because every added channel brings in extra customers

rubric: Channels reach audiences in different contexts and reinforce messages.
Other options state false rules or guarantees.

items.prompt: Which of these statements correctly explain why tracking results matters in a campaign? Select all that apply.

options.label: It helps decide where to move spending
It shows which channels bring the most customers
It proves the campaign goal was set correctly
It makes the ads cheaper without any change

rubric: Tracking reveals channel performance and informs budget shifts.
It does not lower prices by itself or validate the goal choice.

items.prompt: A shop runs two ads for the same product. Ad A was shown 10,000 times and got 300 clicks. Ad B was shown 10,000 times and got 100 clicks. What does this most directly tell the shop?

options.label: Ad B must have had the higher price shown
Ad A had a higher click-through rate
Ad A led to three times as many sales
Ad B was shown to fewer unique people

rubric: Same impressions with more clicks means a higher CTR (3% vs 1%).
Sales, price and reach cannot be inferred from these figures.

items.prompt: Why is an email subscriber list called an "owned" channel?

options.label: Subscribers who opted in are usually more qualified, so the list tends to convert better than most paid channels.
Subscribers on your list can be emailed with relevant offers in most regions without needing explicit consent.
You control access to the audience without paying per message or relying on a platform algorithm.
Email providers rarely filter messages from established senders, so most messages reach the subscriber's inbox.

rubric: Owned means you control the audience relationship rather than renting reach from a platform.
Distractors confuse ownership with guaranteed conversion, consent-free sending or guaranteed delivery.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the difference between SEO and paid search ads?

options.label: SEO earns organic rankings without per-click fees, while paid search charges for each click on an ad.
SEO only works on social platforms, while paid search only appears on the sites you own.
SEO delivers instant traffic once set up, while paid search takes months to build any visits.
SEO charges per click on results, while paid search ranks pages for free based on page quality.

rubric: Organic results are earned through relevance and quality; paid search ads are bought per click.
Distractors reverse the payment models or the speed of results.

items.prompt: What does click-through rate (CTR) measure?

options.label: Clicks divided by impressions
Impressions divided by unique reach
Conversions divided by clicks
Ad spend divided by conversions

rubric: CTR shows how often people who saw an ad clicked it.
Other options describe conversion rate, cost per acquisition and frequency.

items.prompt: Why should a campaign have a clear goal before it launches?

options.label: The goal decides which channel to use, so other channels should never be tested alongside it during the campaign.
The goal fixes the budget for the whole campaign, so spending should not change after launch.
The goal lets you skip tracking, because reaching the target proves each channel worked well.
The goal picks the metric that defines success, so results can be judged and spending adjusted.

rubric: A goal determines what to measure and how to decide where to shift budget.
Distractors treat goals as rigid budgets, a substitute for tracking or a ban on testing.

items.prompt: A retargeting ad is shown only to people who viewed a product page but did not buy. How is it best classified?

options.label: A search tactic that ranks the product page higher in organic results for its keywords
A conversion-focused tactic aimed at people who already showed interest
An awareness tactic meant to introduce the brand to people who have never heard of it
An email tactic that relies on subscribers having already given their address to the brand

rubric: Retargeting reaches warm visitors to push them toward purchase.
Distractors mistake it for awareness advertising, SEO or email.

items.prompt: Which of the following are conversion actions a campaign might track? Select all that apply.

options.label: A newsletter signup
A click on an ad that leads to the site
A completed purchase
An ad impression being served

items.prompt: A coffee shop runs social media ads for its online bean store. Website traffic from social rises 40% in a month, but online sales stay flat. A colleague asks what this most likely means.

options.label: Sales usually lag behind traffic, so the shop should wait another month before reviewing anything.
Visitors are arriving but not buying, so the landing page or offer may not match the ad.
The campaign is working well, since higher traffic shows the ads are reaching the right audience.
Social ads mostly build awareness, so the shop should move its budget to a channel with sales.

rubric: More traffic without more sales suggests a drop-off after the click, such as page or offer mismatch.
Distractors assume traffic equals success, write off the channel or wait without evidence.

items.prompt: A campaign spent $600 and produced 40 purchases. What is the cost per acquisition (CPA)?
rubric: CPA = spend / purchases = 600 / 40 = $15.
Other options invert the division, add the numbers or multiply them.

items.prompt: An ad campaign cost $1,000 and generated $3,000 in revenue. What is its return on ad spend (ROAS)?
rubric: ROAS = revenue / ad spend = 3,000 / 1,000 = 3.0.
Distractors invert the ratio or subtract spend first, which gives profit-style figures.

items.prompt: An ad received 2,500 impressions and 50 clicks. What is the click-through rate?
rubric: Other options come from misplacing the decimal or dividing the wrong way.

items.prompt: Channel A acquires customers at $10 each and Channel B at $25 each; the customers are of similar quality. You must reallocate budget. What is the sensible move?

options.label: Keep the budgets equal, because fairness across channels matters more than the cost of customers.
Move the whole budget to A at once, because CPA will certainly stay at $10 at any spend level.
Shift some budget from B to A and watch whether A's CPA holds as spending grows.
Raise B's budget, because a higher CPA shows that the channel is reaching more valuable people.

rubric: Moving money toward the cheaper channel in steps lets you check that efficiency holds at scale.
Distractors assume CPA never rises, ignore the data or treat high cost as a sign of quality.

items.prompt: You want to A/B test two email subject lines. Which setup gives a fair result?

options.label: Send version A to your best customers and version B to people who have never opened an email.
Send version A with a new image and version B with the old image, plus a different subject line.
Send each version to a random half of the list at the same time, changing only the subject line.
Send version A on Monday to the whole list and version B on Tuesday to the same whole list.

rubric: A fair test randomises the audience, keeps timing equal and changes only one variable.
Distractors vary timing, several elements or audience quality, so the result cannot be attributed to the subject.

items.prompt: You add a link to your spring sale newsletter and want analytics to attribute the visits correctly. Which UTM parameters fit this link? Select all that apply.

options.label: utm_source=newsletter
utm_medium=email
utm_medium=newsletter_spring
utm_campaign=spring_sale

rubric: Source, medium and campaign are standard UTM parameters describing where, how and why the visit came.
utm_budget is not a standard parameter and would not be used for attribution.

items.prompt: A small shop sells a $30 product that leaves $12 margin per sale before ad costs. Its ads currently cost $15 per purchase (ROAS of 2.0). The owner wants to double the ad budget because revenue is twice the spend.

options.label: Keep spending as is, because revenue exceeds ad spend and that proves the campaign is profitable.
Hold off scaling: each sale loses $3 after ad cost, so first lower CPA or raise conversion.
Double the budget now, because any ROAS above 1.0 means the campaign is profitable to scale.
Switch the main goal to impressions, because reach is a safer measure when sales numbers look weak.

rubric: Margin of $12 minus CPA of $15 gives a $3 loss per sale, so scaling would grow losses.
Distractors judge profit by revenue or ROAS alone, ignoring margin, or avoid the problem by changing metric.

items.prompt: A search campaign spent $2,400 and received 3,000 clicks. Its landing page converts 4% of clicks into sales. What is the cost per acquisition (CPA)?
rubric: 4% of 3,000 clicks is 120 sales, and $2,400 divided by 120 is $20.
$0.80 is the cost per click, which confuses CPC with CPA.

items.prompt: A product has a 40% gross margin and is sold only through paid ads. What return on ad spend (ROAS, revenue divided by ad spend) is the break-even point?
rubric: Break-even ROAS is 1 divided by the margin: 1 / 0.4 = 2.5.
0.4 and 4.0 come from using the margin directly or inverting the wrong quantity.

items.prompt: An email list has 20,000 subscribers and you want to test two subject lines before the main send. Which setup is sound?

options.label: Send each version to a random 1,000-person slice, compare open rates, then send the winner to the other 18,000
Send version A on Monday to 10,000 people and B on Friday to the other 10,000, then keep the better day's subject line
Send both versions to the 1,000 most engaged subscribers, pick the one with more opens, then send it to the other 19,000
Send version A to the first 10,000 names alphabetically and B to the last 10,000, then compare total clicks across both halves

rubric: A random, equal test slice isolates the subject line, and the winner is then sent only to the untested remainder.
The other options use non-random groups, confound send day, or send twice to the tested people.

items.prompt: You are tagging a newsletter link for a March sale so analytics can report it correctly. Which UTM parameter set follows standard convention?

options.label: `?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Email`
`?utm_source=newsletter&utm_campaign=march_sale&utm_content=email`
`?utm_source=email&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=march_sale`
`?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=march_sale`

rubric: Source names where the traffic comes from, medium names the channel type, and campaign names the promotion.
Distractors swap source and medium, mislabel the campaign, or omit the medium.

items.prompt: Search ads yield a CPA of $30 and social ads a CPA of $50, against a target CPA of $40. Both channels have ample room to scale. Which budget adjustment follows from the data?

options.label: Move part of the social budget to search in steps, then re-check both CPAs after the next reporting period
Keep both budgets equal, since each channel is bringing in sales and equal funding gives a clean comparison next month
Move all social budget to search at once, since search has the lower CPA and will hold that CPA at any spend level
Raise the social budget, since a CPA above the target shows the channel needs more spend to reach its potential

rubric: Shifting gradually toward the channel beating the target lets you watch for rising marginal cost.
Distractors assume CPA stays constant at scale, ignore the data, or treat a high CPA as a reason to spend more.

items.prompt: Your goal is to increase online sales from an email campaign. Which metrics directly track progress toward that goal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Revenue per recipient
Hours the team spent designing templates
Click-to-purchase conversion rate
Search ad impression share
Facebook page follower count

rubric: Revenue per recipient and click-to-purchase conversion measure sales outcomes of the emails.
Followers, impression share and design hours do not measure email sales.

items.prompt: You plan a $5,000 campaign with 60% to search at $2 per click and 40% to social at $0.80 per click. The landing page converts 5% of search clicks and 2% of social clicks. How many total conversions should you expect?
rubric: 140 comes from applying a blended 3.5% rate to all 4,000 clicks, ignoring the different click mix.

items.prompt: A search ad has an 8% click-through rate but only 0.3% of clicks buy. The ad promises 'Free shipping on all orders' and links to a homepage where free shipping applies only above $100. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The ad's shipping promise contradicts the page, so clicking visitors leave without buying
The 8% click-through rate is unusually high, which suggests much of the traffic is automated clicks from bots
The bid is too low, so the ad shows in poor positions and draws low-quality clicks from casual browsers
The keywords are too broad, so the ad reaches many people who click out of curiosity and never intend to buy

rubric: A strong CTR with weak conversion points to the post-click experience, and the shipping promise contradicts the page.
Distractors blame targeting, position or CTR itself, none of which fit the evidence.

items.prompt: After importing 15,000 purchased contacts, an email program's open rate fell from 30% to 14% and spam complaints rose from 0.02% to 0.4%. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Low-intent contacts are generating complaints that damage sender reputation, so more mail lands in spam
Open rate is distorted by image blocking in many email clients, so the fall is a measurement artifact and not a real change in engagement
Subscribers are tired of the content, so the original list is unsubscribing and opens fall in proportion to the lost audience
The subject lines changed after the import, so the drop reflects weaker copywriting rather than anything about list quality

rubric: The timing and the complaint spike point to list quality and reputation, which depress inbox placement for everyone.
Distractors ignore the complaint rate or offer causes unrelated to the import.

items.prompt: Last-click reporting credits branded search with 70% of sales and social ads with 5%. When social ads were paused for a month, branded search sales fell by 25%. What does this best indicate?

options.label: Social ads were wasting budget, since last-click shows they directly produced only 5% of sales
Branded search sales are independent of social, so the drop was caused by seasonal timing alone
Branded search is the stronger channel, so its budget should rise to make up for the lost sales
Social ads drove demand that later became branded searches, so last-click undervalues social

rubric: The drop in branded search after pausing social shows social fed the later searches that last-click credited elsewhere.
Distractors take last-click credit at face value or assume no link between channels.

items.prompt: In an A/B test of a landing page, version A converted 19 of 400 visitors and version B converted 21 of 400. A colleague wants to roll out B now. What is the soundest analysis?

options.label: B is ahead by about 10% in relative terms, so B is the winner because any positive lift shows a real visitor preference
The gap is two conversions, within random variation, so keep the test running until the sample supports a conclusion
The test is invalid, because each version needs at least 1,000 visitors in total before any result can be counted as evidence
Both versions converted below 10%, so the test shows neither page works well and both should be replaced with new designs

rubric: A two-conversion difference on 400 visitors each is easily produced by chance.
Distractors treat any lead as significant, invent a rigid threshold, or judge by absolute rate.

items.prompt: Over three weeks, a social campaign aimed at a 20,000-person audience shows frequency rising from 2 to 9, click-through rate falling from 1.8% to 0.6%, and CPA rising 70%. Tracking is confirmed working. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A broken conversion pixel, since a tracking fault typically shows as falling click-through rates and rising CPA
Audience saturation and creative fatigue, as the same people see the same ads repeatedly and stop responding
Normal seasonal decline, because all channels lose click-through at the same rate over three weeks
Bids that are too low, since a lower bid reduces reach and therefore raises how often each person sees ads

rubric: High frequency on a small audience with falling CTR is the classic pattern of fatigue.
A pixel fault would not lower CTR, and lower bids would lower frequency rather than raise it.

items.prompt: A campaign reports a ROAS of 4.0, yet the business lost money on it. Which factors could explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Many reported buyers were existing customers who would have bought without the ad
Gross margin on the products was under 25%, so revenue overstates profit
Returns and refunds were not subtracted from the reported revenue
The ads were shown on both mobile and desktop devices
The campaign's click-through rate was above the industry average

rubric: Low margin, non-incremental buyers and unadjusted refunds each make ROAS overstate real profit.
CTR level and device mix do not create a gap between ROAS and profit.

items.prompt: A retailer's report shows paid search: $4,000 spend, 100 sales; email: $300 spend, 60 sales; social: $1,500 spend, 30 sales. The manager proposes moving all paid budget to email because its cost per sale is lowest. What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

options.label: Email's low cost depends on a list built by other channels, so extra spend cannot buy sales at the same cost
Email sales are worth less than other sales, since customers reached by email always buy lower-priced items
Cost per sale is the wrong measure, so channels should be ranked only by the total number of sales delivered
Social should receive the money instead, since its low sales count shows the most unused room to grow

rubric: Email's average cost reflects an existing audience, so marginal spend cannot scale at that cost and depends on other channels feeding the list.
Distractors reject cost-based comparison outright or make unsupported claims about order value.

items.prompt: A paid search campaign adds several broad match keywords. Over the next two weeks click-through rate rises, but conversion rate and cost per acquisition both get worse. Which diagnosis best fits this pattern?

options.label: Conversion tracking is double-counting some clicks, so the reported rate fell even though visitor behaviour is unchanged
Broad match is pulling in loosely related queries that click readily but don't match what the offer actually sells
The added keywords placed ads in lower positions, where visitors are known to be much less likely to purchase
Higher click volume has pushed Quality Score up, which raises ad costs and cuts the share of buyers who convert

rubric: Rising CTR with falling conversion points to less-qualified traffic, which broad match commonly brings.
Distractors invent Quality Score or position effects, or blame tracking, without evidence in the pattern.

items.prompt: A newsletter's open rate jumps from 22% to 41% after a mail-client privacy update, while clicks per send and site sessions from email stay flat. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: The subject line improved enough to double interest, which would normally have lifted clicks by a similar proportion
A better send time boosted opens sharply, and clicks stayed flat because clicks depend only on the offer itself
Mail clients that pre-load images are registering automatic opens, so open rate no longer reflects human attention
A list-cleaning step removed inactive addresses, which always raises opens while leaving click totals unchanged

rubric: Automatic pre-loading inflates opens without changing clicks, so open rate becomes unreliable.
Other options explain the jump with real engagement changes that would also move clicks.

items.prompt: In a last-click attribution report, branded search gets most conversions and display gets almost none, though display spend is large. What is the most accurate reading of this data?

options.label: Last-click spreads credit evenly across all touchpoints, so branded search must simply have had the most touches overall
Display clicks rarely convert, so the low last-click credit shows display impressions have no influence on purchases
Branded search often captures demand that display created earlier, but last-click credits only the final touch
Branded search is the highest-intent audience, so its share of conversions proves it generates most of the new demand

rubric: Last-click gives all credit to the final touch, so brand search can capture demand created by upper-funnel channels.
Distractors treat last-click credit as proof of causation or misdescribe how the model works.

items.prompt: A retargeting campaign reports a ROAS of 5.0. When it is paused for three weeks, total store revenue barely changes. What explains this best?

options.label: A ROAS of 5.0 is below the usual retargeting benchmark, so the campaign was too weak to matter either way
Pausing retargeting reset the learning of other campaigns, which wiped out the revenue the retargeting had been producing
Retargeting impressions were low, which means ROAS can't be trusted at small spend levels and revenue is unaffected
Retargeting mostly reached people already likely to buy, so its attributed ROAS overstated the revenue it truly caused

rubric: Revenue not falling when spend stops indicates low incrementality: the buyers would have purchased anyway.
Distractors blame learning resets, benchmarks or spend size rather than the gap between attributed and caused revenue.

items.prompt: A marketer ran a subject-line A/B test, checked results daily, and stopped after two days when variant B first showed 95% significance. Which statement best identifies the flaw?

options.label: Open-rate significance is a weak proxy for subject-line quality, so the test should have compared revenue per email before any winner was declared
Stopping at the first significant reading inflates false positives, so the winner may be noise; fix sample size in advance
A 95% confidence level means variant B has a 95% chance of beating the control on future sends, so the early result is reliable
Two days is too short because open behaviour differs by weekday, so the test should have run a full month before any result counted

rubric: Repeated peeking with early stopping raises the false-positive rate; the stopping rule must be set beforehand.
Distractors misread confidence levels or impose arbitrary duration rules.

items.prompt: Reported conversions for a campaign dropped 50% overnight, and the team suspects a tracking fault rather than a real fall in demand. Which checks would help separate the two explanations? Select all that apply.

options.label: Check whether social follower growth slowed in the same week
Compare ad click counts against analytics sessions to see whether the tags still fire
Check whether the drop appears across every channel right after a recent site release
Compare conversions reported by the ad platform with backend orders for the same dates
Compare ad click-through rates before and after the drop

rubric: Backend orders, cross-channel timing and click-to-session gaps all isolate measurement faults from demand changes.
CTR and follower growth say little about whether conversion tags are working.

items.prompt: A brand runs paid search, email and paid social. Paid social sessions doubled this month, but its conversion rate is now the lowest of any channel and bounce rate is 85%. Desktop sessions from social still convert normally. Which analysis most directly isolates the cause?

options.label: Compare social spend against email list growth to see whether the audiences are overlapping with subscribers
Segment paid social conversions by device and landing page to check whether mobile visitors hit a weak page
Compare overall bounce rate across all three channels to see whether social is simply a lower-quality channel
Compare this month's social impressions with last month's to see whether reach growth diluted audience quality

rubric: Normal desktop conversion suggests the problem is device-specific, so segmenting by device and landing page finds it.
Channel-level or reach comparisons mask the device split that the data already hints at.

items.prompt: Goal: minimise blended cost per acquisition. Search has an average CPA of $20, but its last $1,000 of spend returned a CPA of $60. Paid social has an average CPA of $35 and a marginal CPA of $30. Which budget decision is best against that goal?

options.label: Move budget from search to social, as long as social's marginal CPA stays below the marginal CPA of the search spend removed
Raise both budgets equally, because equal growth keeps the channel mix stable and so protects the blended CPA
Keep budgets fixed, because search has the lowest average CPA and so remains the most efficient place for every extra dollar
Cut social entirely, since its average CPA is higher than search and averages show where the money works hardest

rubric: Budget should follow marginal, not average, CPA; shifting continues until marginal costs are about equal.
Distractors rely on average CPA or on keeping the mix constant.

items.prompt: A B2B firm with a three-month sales cycle launches a LinkedIn campaign and must report on it after six weeks. Judged on being both meaningful and measurable by then, which primary KPI is best?

options.label: Impressions and follower growth, because awareness is the earliest signal and the easiest to measure reliably
Closed-won revenue and ROAS, because they are the true business outcome and the only figures finance accepts
Click-through rate on ads, because it shows creative quality and responds within days of launch
Cost per marketing-qualified lead, together with the early lead-to-opportunity rate of the first cohorts

rubric: Leading indicators tied to pipeline are available inside six weeks and still relate to revenue.
Closed-won revenue lags too far; impressions and CTR are not linked to qualified demand.

items.prompt: A colleague proposes pausing all brand-term search ads because the company already ranks first organically for them. Judged on protecting revenue and spending efficiently, which response is best?

options.label: Approve it, since organic first place already captures brand clicks and paid ads duplicate them
Reject it, since brand ads lift Quality Score on non-brand keywords and pausing them raises account costs
Run a holdout test pausing brand ads in some regions, since competitors may bid on the brand name
Approve it if the ads never name competitors, since competitor bidding is then the only risk to revenue

rubric: Incrementality of brand ads is uncertain and testable; a holdout measures real lost clicks and revenue.
Distractors assume full organic capture or invent an absolute rule.

items.prompt: To lift sales fast, a retailer can email a purchased list of 50,000 addresses or re-engage its own 8,000-subscriber list in segments. Criteria: protect sender reputation and stay compliant with consent rules. Which option is best?

options.label: Email the purchased list with a strong discount, because a better offer outweighs missing consent and lowers complaints
Re-engage the owned list in segments and suspend long-inactive contacts, as consented addresses protect deliverability
Send to the full owned list weekly, since higher frequency re-engages inactive contacts and improves engagement signals
Email the purchased list at low volume, because small sends keep complaint counts too low for providers to notice

rubric: Consented, segmented sending protects reputation and compliance; purchased lists risk spam traps and complaints.
Distractors assume volume control or offers can offset lack of consent, or that frequency fixes inactivity.

items.prompt: A small shop spends $3,000 a month and gets about 40 conversions. It wants to learn which channel to fund. Judged on reliability given this limited data, which measurement approach is best?

options.label: Build a multi-touch data-driven attribution model, because it divides credit most precisely across every channel and touchpoint
Use UTM-tagged tracking and change one channel's budget at a time, because small volumes can't support complex models
Judge channels by monthly impressions, because reach is stable at low volumes while conversions are too noisy to use
Rely on platform-reported conversions alone, because each platform sees its own clicks and so knows its own results best

rubric: With few conversions, simple consistent tracking and one-change-at-a-time tests are more reliable than complex models.
Distractors prefer sophistication, self-reporting platforms or reach metrics that miss the business goal.

items.prompt: A team must decide whether to roll out the winner of a creative A/B test across all ad budgets. Which are sound criteria for judging the result? Select all that apply.

options.label: The primary metric was tied to the goal, such as CPA, rather than clicks alone
The sample size and duration were set before launch and reached
The test ended once one variant first pulled ahead
The variant with the highest click-through rate wins whatever its conversions
The test covered at least one full weekly cycle to absorb day-of-week effects

rubric: Predefined sample, goal-linked metric and full weekly cycles make the result trustworthy.
Click-only winners and early stopping risk rolling out noise or irrelevant gains.

items.prompt: A retailer has $20,000 for Black Friday. Criteria: blended ROAS of at least 3.0 and many new customers. Retargeting returns ROAS 7 but its audience can absorb only $4,000 before returns collapse. Prospecting returns ROAS 2.2 and is the only source of new customers. Which plan best meets the criteria?

options.label: Split $10,000 each, because an even split balances new and existing customers and hedges the risk
Put all $20,000 into retargeting, because its ROAS is highest and so gives the best blended return
Put all $20,000 into prospecting, because new customers matter most and its ROAS is close enough to the target
Cap retargeting at $4,000 and put the other $16,000 into prospecting, for a blended ROAS near 3.2

rubric: Capping retargeting at its limit and putting the rest in prospecting yields about 63,200 revenue, so blended ROAS is roughly 3.16.
Other plans overspend a saturated audience, miss the 3.0 ROAS, or ignore diminishing returns.

items.prompt: A retailer's branded search campaign shows 12x ROAS on last-click. The team wants to move budget from prospecting social to branded search. Which critique of this plan is strongest?

options.label: A 12x ROAS is too high to be real for search, so tracking is probably faulty; audit the tags before using any channel data to move budget.
Branded search mostly captures demand other channels created, so last-click inflates its value; a geo holdout would show true lift.
Last-click undervalues social, so social should be credited at branded search's ROAS and the budget split kept equal between the two channels.
Branded search has the best ROAS, so it should get the next dollar; cap spend only once its cost per click starts to rise noticeably.

rubric: Branded queries usually come from people already persuaded elsewhere, so last-click credit overstates incrementality.
Distractors treat observed ROAS as causal or dismiss the data instead of testing incrementality.

items.prompt: An email team tested two subject lines on 2,000 recipients each. They checked results daily and stopped when p first fell to 0.04. Which judgement of the result is best?

options.label: Daily peeking with early stopping inflates false positives, so confirm with a fixed sample size or a sequential correction.
The test is invalid because open rates are unreliable, so only click-through can ever be used to declare a winner.
The p-value should be halved because two variants were compared, which makes the result stronger and confirms the winner.
The result is reliable, because p=0.04 is below 0.05 and 2,000 recipients per arm is large enough for any email test.

rubric: Repeatedly testing and stopping at first significance raises the real false-positive rate well above 5%.
Distractors accept the nominal p-value or invent unrelated corrections.

items.prompt: Goal: maximise total conversions within a fixed budget. Channel A has average CPA $20 but marginal CPA $55 at current spend. Channel B has average CPA $35 but marginal CPA $30. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Shift budget from B to A, since A's lower average CPA shows it is the more efficient channel at any level of spend.
Keep budget on A, since its lower average CPA is the right basis for deciding where the next dollar should be spent.
Shift budget from A to B, since B's lower marginal CPA means each moved dollar buys more, until marginal CPAs roughly equalise.
Split budget equally, since the average CPAs are in the same range and diversification reduces overall risk to the plan.

rubric: Optimal allocation equalises marginal returns, not average returns.
Distractors rely on average CPA, ignoring diminishing returns.

items.prompt: A subscription app must choose which acquisition channel to scale. Criteria: cash payback within 12 months, and allowance for churn differing by channel. Which evaluation approach is strongest?

options.label: Rank channels by click-through rate, since stronger ad engagement shows the audience values the product most highly and will stay subscribed.
Rank channels by cost per install, since installs are the earliest signal and cheaper installs lead to more paying subscribers per dollar.
Compare cohorts on cumulative margin per user against CAC, and scale channels that recover cost within a year.
Rank channels by first-month conversion rate, since early conversion predicts retention equally well across all acquisition sources.

rubric: Cohort margin versus CAC directly tests the payback and churn criteria.
Distractors use upstream proxies that ignore retention and margin.

items.prompt: Privacy changes cut user-level tracking by about 40%. Criteria: decisions must stay credible to finance and must not depend on one platform's self-reported numbers. Which measurement approach is best?

options.label: Switch wholly to last-click in web analytics, since it is deterministic and unaffected by the privacy changes described.
Rely on each platform's modelled conversions, since their algorithms fill the gaps better than any independent method can.
Triangulate with marketing mix modelling and periodic lift tests, using the tests to calibrate the model and platform figures.
Stop measuring channels individually and judge only total sales, since channel analysis is no longer possible at all.

rubric: Combining MMM with experiments gives independent, calibrated evidence.
Distractors trust one biased source or abandon channel-level measurement.

items.prompt: A brand proposes judging an influencer campaign only by redemptions of each influencer's promo code. Which are valid criticisms of this plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: Influencers paid a flat fee make redemption counts invalid for any purpose, even comparing creators.
Some redeemers would have bought anyway, so redemptions do not measure incremental sales.
Viewers who buy later without using the code are missed, so impact is understated.
Codes leak to coupon sites, so redemptions include buyers the influencer never influenced.
Promo codes cannot be linked to revenue in any system, so redemptions have no financial meaning.

rubric: Leakage, unattributed purchases and non-incremental buyers all weaken code redemptions as a measure.
Codes can be tied to revenue and still allow rough comparison, so the other two claims are overstated.

items.prompt: After moving a retailer's search budget to an automated campaign type, the agency reports blended CPA down 30%. Your data shows new-customer share of conversions fell from 60% to 20%, with revenue flat. The goal was customer growth. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Likely false efficiency: spend shifted toward existing customers, so judge on new-customer CPA and incremental lift before scaling.
Success: CPA fell 30%, which is the agreed efficiency metric, so the budget should be expanded without further checks.
Failure: any fall in new-customer share proves the automation is broken, so it should be switched off immediately.
Inconclusive: revenue is flat, so nothing changed, and both the CPA and customer mix movements should be treated as noise.

rubric: The CPA gain likely comes from harvesting existing customers, which conflicts with the growth goal.
Distractors ignore the goal, overreact, or dismiss a large mix shift as noise.

items.prompt: Design a test of paid social's incremental sales. Constraints: no user-level tracking, spend cannot be stopped nationwide, results within 8 weeks. Which design fits every constraint?

options.label: Compare platform-reported conversions across two audiences, since the platform's attribution already isolates the incremental effect.
Compare sales before and after doubling spend nationwide, since a pre-post comparison needs no holdout and finishes within 8 weeks.
Match regions on past sales, pause or cut ads in a random subset, and compare sales against the remaining regions over the period.
Survey customers on whether they saw the ads, then credit paid social with every sale from those who said yes.

rubric: A matched-market geo holdout needs no user tracking and keeps spend running elsewhere.
Distractors confound with time, rely on recall, or trust platform attribution.

items.prompt: Design a launch plan for a B2B software firm. Constraints: $30k budget, 90-day sales cycle, and the board wants a credible leading indicator by week 4. Which plan satisfies all of them?

options.label: Run broad awareness ads, judge by impressions at week 4, and judge pipeline at day 90 before changing any budget.
Put all spend into retargeting in week one, and judge by closed revenue at week 4 as proof the plan is working.
Optimise for lowest cost per lead from a gated ebook across search and social, report lead volume at week 4 as proof of pipeline, and review sales at day 90.
Target named accounts on search and LinkedIn, track qualified meetings booked at week 4, and review pipeline at day 90.

rubric: Qualified meetings are a leading indicator tied to pipeline within the 90-day cycle.
Distractors use vanity metrics, impossible closed revenue, or low-quality lead volume.

items.prompt: Design measurement for a retailer's weekly promo email to show incremental revenue. Constraints: a 40,000-person list, no noticeable revenue harm, and results reusable week to week. Which design is best?

options.label: Compare revenue from openers against non-openers, since openers have shown the intent that the email itself created.
Suppress a random 10% of the list from promos persistently, and compare revenue per subscriber against the mailed 90%.
Send to everyone and compare this week's revenue with last week's, adjusting for the change in list size.
Hold out the least engaged 10% of subscribers, since they are cheapest to withhold and give a clean baseline.

rubric: A random persistent holdout gives an unbiased, reusable estimate at low cost.
Distractors compare self-selected or non-comparable groups.

items.prompt: A lead-gen advertiser's platform optimises toward form fills, but only 8% of leads become sales-qualified. Constraints: a cost-per-qualified-lead cap and no extra form fields. Which change meets them?

options.label: Cut daily budgets by 80% so the platform shows ads only to the best prospects, while still optimising on form fills.
Add more form fields to filter low-intent users, since longer forms raise intent while keeping the cost per lead about the same.
Import CRM stage data back to the ad platform, optimise toward qualified-lead events, and judge campaigns on cost per qualified lead.
Raise bids on all campaigns so the platform reaches higher-intent users, while still optimising on form fills as before.

rubric: Feeding back qualified-lead events retrains optimisation on the real goal without changing the form.
Distractors break the no-extra-fields rule or leave the optimisation signal unchanged.

items.prompt: Design a remarketing setup for a mattress brand. Purchases recur about every 8 years, consideration lasts about 30 days, and budget per prospect is capped. Which setup fits?

options.label: Target past buyers with new-product ads for 365 days, since existing customers convert at the highest rate.
Target only checkout abandoners for 3 days, since only they have intent and every other visitor is wasted spend.
Target all site visitors for 180 days with no frequency cap, since a long window catches the rare buyer when ready.
Target visitors for 30 days with a frequency cap, exclude purchasers, and tier creative by pages viewed.

rubric: The window matches consideration, caps respect budget, and purchaser exclusion avoids waste on an 8-year cycle.
Distractors ignore the cycle, the cap, or discard viable mid-funnel prospects.

items.prompt: Which elements belong in a pre-agreed rule for reallocating budget between channels so that it is robust to noise and platform bias? Select all that apply.

options.label: A minimum data volume and review period before any move, set before the data is seen.
Daily moves toward whichever channel shows the highest in-platform ROAS.
Comparison on marginal returns, calibrated against periodic incrementality tests.
A cap on how much budget can shift in one step, so a misread signal is cheap to reverse.
Equal spend across all channels regardless of results, to keep the comparison fair.

rubric: Pre-set thresholds, marginal and calibrated returns, and capped steps make reallocation robust.
Chasing daily platform ROAS amplifies noise and bias; fixed equal spend ignores results.

items.prompt: A furniture retailer's campaign plan sets a ROAS goal, channel mix, budgets and UTM tags. Purchases typically happen about 21 days after the first ad click, yet the plan cuts underperforming campaigns after 7 days. What is the plan missing?

options.label: A reporting window matched to the 21-day conversion lag, or a validated leading metric, before any cut decisions are made.
A higher ROAS goal, since a stricter target would force underperforming campaigns to show themselves within the first week.
A larger number of channels, since adding more channels spreads the risk of the 7-day review cutting winning campaigns.
More UTM parameters, since extra tagging would let first-week data predict later purchases without needing to wait.

rubric: Decisions must be made on data that covers the conversion lag, or on a validated proxy.
Distractors add channels, targets or tags that do nothing about the lag.
